name: Dummy Deck
description: Sandbox for testing new technical phrases before migration.

cards.sideA: compileSdkVersion indica la versión de Android con la que se compila la app.

sideB.text: compileSdkVersion sets the Android version used to compile the app.
compileSdkVersion indicates which Android version the app is compiled with.
compileSdkVersion defines the Android version that compiles the app.
compileSdkVersion defines the Android version against which the app is compiled.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~...sets the Android version is compiled the app~ lacks the proper sentence structure. It needs a relative clause and a preposition at the end, such as [the Android version the app is compiled with].

~...against the app is compiled~ is missing the relative pronoun. You must use [against which the app is compiled].

~...sets the Android version with the app gets compiled~ is missing a relative pronoun. You must say [with which the app gets compiled] or leave the preposition at the end: [the app gets compiled with].

~...sets the Android version the app is compiled~ leaves the clause unfinished. 'Compile' needs its preposition, so the sentence has to close with it: [the Android version the app is compiled with].

~...sets the Android version which the app is compiled~ adds the pronoun but still drops the preposition. Both options are valid: [which the app is compiled with] or [with which the app is compiled].

cards.sideA: Es la versión de Android contra la que la app se construye y se prueba.

sideB.text: It's the Android version the app is built and tested against.
That's the Android version used to build and test the app.
It's the Android version against which the app is built and tested.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~It is the Android version against the app is built and tested~ is missing the relative pronoun. A fronted preposition always drags [which] along with it: [the Android version against which the app is built and tested]. Leaving the preposition at the end is the only position where the pronoun may disappear: [the Android version the app is built and tested against].

cards.sideA: Kotlin es el lenguaje en el que está escrito el lado Android de la app.

sideB.text: Kotlin is the language the Android side of the app is written in.
Kotlin is the language used to write the Android side of the app.
The Android side of the app is written in Kotlin.
Kotlin is the language the Android app is written in.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~...the Android app is written~ is incomplete. You must include the preposition [in] at the end: [is written in].

~Kotlin is the language written in the Android side of the app~ reverses the meaning: it says the language itself was written inside the Android side. What gets written is the code, so the relative clause must keep its own subject: [the language the Android side of the app is written in].

cards.sideA: La correspondencia de Gradle en iOS se gestiona directamente en Xcode.

sideB.text: On iOS, the equivalent of Gradle is handled directly in Xcode.
The iOS counterpart of Gradle is handled directly inside Xcode.
On iOS, whatever Gradle does is managed straight from Xcode.
On iOS, the equivalent of Gradle is handled directly by Xcode.

cards.note:
~...the corresponcy of Gradle~ is incorrect because 'corresponcy' is not a valid word. The correct terms are [equivalent] or [counterpart].

[in Xcode] presents Xcode as the place where the work happens, while [by Xcode] presents it as the agent doing the work. Both are natural in a passive sentence like this one.

cards.sideA: El código elige el spinner según la plataforma en la que corre.

sideB.text: The code picks the spinner based on the platform it runs on.
The code chooses the spinner depending on the platform it is running on.
Which spinner is used depends on the platform the code runs on.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~...based on the platform it runs~ is incomplete. You must include the preposition [on] at the end to specify where it runs: [it runs on].

In this context, 'run on' is not a true phrasal verb. It is simply the verb [run] (to execute or operate) followed by the preposition [on] indicating the platform or surface. The core meaning of the verb does not change idiomatically as it would in a real phrasal verb like 'run out' or 'run into'.

cards.sideA: VSCode es solo el editor donde escribo el código; quien compila es Android y Xcode por detrás.

sideB.text: VSCode is only the editor where I write the code; Android and Xcode do the compiling behind it.
VSCode is just the editor I write the code in; the actual compiling is done by Android and Xcode.
I only use VSCode to write the code; Android and Xcode are the ones compiling in the background.
VSCode is only the editor where I write the code; it's Android and Xcode that compile behind it.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~...who compiles is Android and Xcode behind it~ is incorrect because 'who' is used for people. For tools or programs, use [what compiles] or [the ones that compile].

~It's Android and Xcode that compiles behind it~ fails the agreement. The focus of the cleft is two tools, so the verb stays plural: [it's Android and Xcode that compile behind it].

~It's Android and Xcode they ones that compiled behind it~ mixes two different structures and puts the verb in the past. Choose one: [it's Android and Xcode that compile behind it] or [Android and Xcode are the ones that compile behind it].

~...the ones which compiles are Android and Xcode behind it~ breaks the agreement and the word order. The plural head needs a plural verb and the object comes before the complement: [the ones that compile it are Android and Xcode].

~...which compiles it is Android and Xcode~ cannot open a clause with 'which'. A free relative working as the subject takes [what]: [what compiles it is Android and Xcode].

cards.sideA: Ese vacío heredado ya no ocurre; esta línea lo restaura.

sideB.text: That inherited blank state no longer happens; this line restores it.
That inherited empty state does not happen anymore; this line resets it.
The inherited blank value no longer occurs, because this line restores it.
That inherited blank state is not happening anymore; this line restores it.

cards.note:
~That inherited gap no longer happens~ changes the meaning. In programming, 'vacío' refers to a [blank state] or [empty value], whereas 'gap' refers to physical or temporal space.

~That inherited blank state is no longer happened~ puts an intransitive verb into the passive. 'Happen' never takes a passive form because nobody performs it on something else: [no longer happens] or [does not happen anymore].

[Is not happening anymore] is valid because the verb stays active. The continuous points at the current situation, while [no longer happens] states the general fact.

cards.sideA: Acabo de enviártelo por chat.

sideB.text: I just sent it to you on chat.
I just sent it to you over chat.
I have just sent it to you through chat.

cards.note: ~I just sent it to you by chat~ is not idiomatic. [By] pairs with a closed set of channel nouns such as by email, by phone, by mail, or by fax. 'Chat' is not part of that set and takes [on chat], [over chat], [through chat], or [via chat].

cards.sideA: El archivo pubspec.lock registra las versiones exactas de las dependencias de la app.

sideB.text: The pubspec.lock file records the exact versions of the app's dependencies.
The pubspec.lock file keeps the exact versions of the app's dependencies.
pubspec.lock stores the exact dependency versions used by the app.
The pubspec.lock file records the exact dependency versions of the app.

cards.note: ~The pubspec.lock file registers the exact versions dependencies of the app~ has two problems. [Register] in English means to sign up or enroll a person, so for a file that keeps a list the verb is [records], [keeps], or [stores]. Two nouns also cannot be stacked as ~versions dependencies~: use [the exact dependency versions] or [the exact versions of the dependencies].

cards.sideA: Un bug es un error en un programa.

sideB.text: A bug is an error in a program.
A bug is a mistake in a program.
A bug is a flaw in a program.

cards.note:
~A bug is an error of a program~ sounds unnatural because the error is located inside the program, it is not something the program possesses. Use [an error in a program], or compress it into a single noun phrase as [a program error]. The pattern with [of] works for parts or properties, as in [the size of the file] or [the name of the variable], not for the place where a problem occurs.

~A bug is an error from a program~ fails for a similar reason. [From] marks origin or source, so it suggests the program emitted the error toward something else, as in [an error message from the server]. The bug is not coming out of the program, it lives inside it, so the preposition stays [in].

cards.sideA: Porque es un requisito de iOS, cada año es lo mismo.

sideB.text: Because it's an iOS requirement; it's the same every year.
Because iOS requires it, and it's the same every year.
Because it's a requirement from iOS; every year it's the same.
Because it's a requirement for iOS; every year it's the same.

cards.sideA: Un firewall es un guardia digital que bloquea datos sospechosos.

sideB.text: A firewall is a digital guard that blocks suspicious data.
A firewall acts as a digital guard that blocks suspicious data.
A firewall is like a digital security guard that blocks suspicious data.

cards.sideA: Un firewall es una muralla que protege tu red.

sideB.text: A firewall is a wall that protects your network.
A firewall is a barrier that protects your network.
A firewall works as a wall that shields your network.

cards.sideA: Un firewall es un guardián de conexiones de red.

sideB.text: A firewall is a guardian of network connections.
A firewall is a gatekeeper for network connections.
A firewall guards the network connections.

cards.note: ~A firewall is a guardian in a network connections~ breaks twice. The article [a] cannot sit in front of a plural noun, and [in] places the firewall inside the connections instead of watching over them. The guardian relationship is expressed with [of] or [for]: [a guardian of network connections], [a gatekeeper for network connections].

cards.sideA: Un firewall personal permite todo el tráfico por defecto.

sideB.text: A personal firewall allows all traffic by default.
A personal firewall lets all traffic through by default.
By default, a personal firewall permits all traffic.

cards.sideA: Un firewall personal protege un solo dispositivo.

sideB.text: A personal firewall protects a single device.
A personal firewall only protects one device.
A personal firewall guards just one device.

cards.sideA: Un firewall personal es un programa sencillo en tu computadora.

sideB.text: A personal firewall is a simple program on your computer.
A personal firewall is just a simple program running on your computer.
A personal firewall is a lightweight program installed on your computer.

cards.note: ~A personal firewall is an easy program on your computer~ shifts the meaning to how much effort the program takes to use. The point here is that it is not complex, so use [simple], [basic] or [lightweight]. [Easy] describes a task or an experience, as in [an easy task] or [the app is easy to use], not the internal complexity of a thing.

cards.sideA: Un firewall de empresa bloquea todo el tráfico por defecto para máxima seguridad.

sideB.text: A corporate firewall blocks all traffic by default for maximum security.
A corporate firewall denies all traffic by default for maximum security.
For maximum security, a corporate firewall blocks all traffic by default.
A corporate firewall blocks all traffic by default to maximize security.

cards.sideA: Un firewall de empresa inspecciona el contenido de datos de miles de usuarios a la vez.

sideB.text: A corporate firewall inspects the data content of thousands of users at once.
A corporate firewall inspects the data of thousands of users at the same time.
A corporate firewall scans the data content of thousands of users simultaneously.

cards.sideA: A un firewall de empresa debes decirle explícitamente en quién confiar.

sideB.text: A corporate firewall must be explicitly told who to trust.
You must explicitly tell a corporate firewall who to trust.
With a corporate firewall, you have to state explicitly who to trust.

cards.sideA: Al hacer checkout, la Cotización se convierte en una Orden de Venta.

sideB.text: When you check out, the Quote becomes a Sales Order.
At checkout, the Quote is converted into a Sales Order.
Once the checkout is done, the Quote turns into a Sales Order.

cards.note: ~When Checking out, the Quote becomes a Sales Order~ makes the Quote the one doing the checking out, because a reduced [when + -ing] clause borrows the subject of the main clause. Since the person checking out and the thing being converted are different, the subject must stay explicit: [when you check out], or the verb can be dropped entirely: [at checkout].

cards.sideA: ¿Puedes destacar el código que se ha modificado?

sideB.text: Can you highlight the code that has been modified?
Could you highlight the code that changed?
Can you point out the modified code?
Can you highlight the code that was modified?

cards.sideA: Si es así, deberíamos salir temprano para evitar el tráfico.

sideB.text: If so, we should leave early to beat the traffic.
If that is the case, we should leave early to avoid the traffic.
If so, we had better leave early to beat the traffic.

cards.sideA: Si es así, necesitamos cancelar la reservación de inmediato.

sideB.text: If that's so, we need to cancel the reservation right away.
If so, we need to cancel the reservation immediately.
If that is the case, we have to cancel the booking right away.

cards.sideA: Si es así, ella se unirá a nosotros para cenar después del trabajo.

sideB.text: If so, she will join us for dinner after work.
If that is the case, she will join us for dinner after work.
If so, she is going to join us for dinner after work.

cards.sideA: Las notificaciones push requieren una conexión a internet para funcionar.

sideB.text: Push notifications require an internet connection to work.
Push notifications need an internet connection in order to work.
Without an internet connection, push notifications do not work.

cards.sideA: Las notificaciones push se muestran en la pantalla del dispositivo.

sideB.text: Push notifications are displayed on the device's screen.
Push notifications show up on the device screen.
Push notifications appear on the screen of the device.

cards.sideA: El usuario debe instalar la aplicación para recibir notificaciones push.

sideB.text: The user must install the app to receive push notifications.
The user has to install the app in order to get push notifications.
To receive push notifications, the user needs to install the app.

cards.sideA: Un SMS no requiere internet para funcionar.

sideB.text: An SMS does not require internet to work.
An SMS does not need an internet connection to work.
Text messages work without internet.

cards.sideA: Las notificaciones SMS llegan directamente al número de teléfono.

sideB.text: SMS notifications arrive directly to the phone number.
SMS notifications go straight to the phone number.
SMS notifications are delivered directly to the phone number.

cards.sideA: Los SMS funcionan en cualquier teléfono móvil básico.

sideB.text: SMS messages work on any basic mobile phone.
Text messages work on any basic cell phone.
SMS works on any simple mobile phone.

cards.sideA: ¿En qué fase estamos?

sideB.text: In which phase are we?
Which phase are we in?
What phase are we in?

cards.sideA: ¿En qué paso estamos?

sideB.text: In which step are we?
Which step are we in?
What step are we on?

cards.sideA: ¿En qué fase y paso estamos?

sideB.text: In which phase and step are we?
Which phase and step are we in?
What phase and step are we on?

cards.sideA: Él realmente no tiene por qué saberlo.

sideB.text: He doesn't really have to know.
He doesn't really need to know.
There's no reason for him to know, really.
He doesn't really have to know it.

cards.note: [Know] can drop its object when the thing known is obvious from context, which is why [he doesn't really have to know] already works on its own. Adding [it] points at one specific piece of information that was just mentioned.

cards.sideA: Nunca he visto ese problema, déjame revisarlo.

sideB.text: I've never seen that problem, let me check it.
I've never run into that issue, let me take a look.
That's a problem I've never seen before, let me check it out.

cards.sideA: Ahora necesitamos incrementar la versión.

sideB.text: Now we need to bump the version.
Now we need to increment the version number.
We have to bump the version now.

cards.sideA: Bounce reinicia un solo servicio.

sideB.text: Bounce restarts a single service.
A bounce restarts just one service.
Bouncing restarts only one service.

cards.sideA: Reboot reinicia el servidor entero.

sideB.text: Reboot restarts the entire server.
A reboot restarts the whole server.
Rebooting restarts the server completely.

cards.sideA: Bounce es rápido; reboot limpia todo.

sideB.text: Bounce is fast; reboot clears everything.
A bounce is quick; a reboot wipes everything clean.
Bouncing is fast, while rebooting clears everything.

cards.sideA: Restart reinicia una aplicación o stack completo.

sideB.text: Restart restarts a full application or stack.
A restart brings back a whole application or stack.
Restarting applies to an entire application or stack.

cards.sideA: Restart es el verbo genérico para cualquier caso.

sideB.text: Restart is the generic verb for any case.
Restart is the general term for any of these cases.
Restart is the catch all verb for every case.

cards.note: ~Restart is the generic verb in any case~ changes the meaning, because [in any case] is a fixed expression that means [anyway] or [regardless of what happens]. To say which situations the verb covers, the preposition has to be [for]: [the generic verb for any case], [the general term for every case].

cards.sideA: Reboot y Bounce son como Restart, pero más especializados.

sideB.text: Reboot and Bounce are like Restart, but more specialized.
Reboot and Bounce work like Restart, only more specific.
Reboot and Bounce are specialized versions of Restart.

cards.sideA: Revisa la línea 374, ¿qué dice?

sideB.text: Check line 374, what does it say?
Take a look at line 374, what does it say?
Go to line 374 and tell me what it says.

cards.sideA: Revisa la línea 287, pégamela en el chat.

sideB.text: Check line 287 and paste it in the chat for me.
Look at line 287 and paste it into the chat.
Go to line 287 and drop it in the chat.

cards.sideA: Estoy buscando la línea 653, te la pegaré en el chat.

sideB.text: I'm looking for line 653, I'll paste it in the chat for you.
I'm searching for line 653, I'll drop it in the chat.
I'm trying to find line 653, I'll paste it into the chat.

cards.sideA: Ok, vuelve a los mensajes de errores y espera un momento ahí.

sideB.text: Ok, go back to the error messages and hold on there for a moment.
Ok, scroll back to the error messages and stay there for a second.
Ok, go back to the error messages and wait there a moment.

cards.sideA: Click derecho en el archivo e inspecciónalo.

sideB.text: Right click on the file and inspect it.
Right click the file and inspect it.
Do a right click on the file and take a look at it.

cards.sideA: Copia el comentario, la primera línea, y pégalo en el otro archivo.

sideB.text: Copy the comment, the first line, and paste it into the other file.
Copy the comment on the first line and paste it in the other file.
Grab the comment, the first line, and paste it into the other file.

cards.sideA: Ellos son sutilmente diferentes.

sideB.text: They are subtly different.
They are slightly different.
There is a subtle difference between them.

cards.sideA: No tengo toda la información.

sideB.text: I don't have the whole picture.
I don't have all the information.
I'm missing part of the picture.

cards.sideA: Lo que está por enviarse.

sideB.text: What is about to be sent.
The thing that is about to be sent.
Whatever is about to be sent.

cards.sideA: Él trabaja como consultor, en una consultora.

sideB.text: He works as a consultant, at a consulting firm.
He works as a consultant for a consultancy.
He is a consultant at a consulting company.

cards.note: ~He works as a consulter, at a consulting firm~ fails because the profession is [consultant]. [Consulter] is not the job title in English; the agent noun for this verb is irregular and ends in -ant, like [assistant], [applicant] or [participant].

cards.sideA: Trabajamos en una consultora, como consultores.

sideB.text: We work at a consulting firm, as consultants.
We work for a consultancy, as consultants.
We are consultants at a consulting company.

cards.sideA: Esta línea lo restaura, o resetea.

sideB.text: This line restores or resets it.
This line either restores it or resets it.
This line restores it, or resets it.

cards.sideA: Esta línea lo resetea o restaura.

sideB.text: This line resets or restores it.
This line either resets it or restores it.
This line resets it, or restores it.

cards.sideA: No he recibido nada, quizás John sí.

sideB.text: I haven't received anything, maybe John has.
I haven't gotten anything, maybe John has.
Nothing has come to me, maybe John has received it.

cards.sideA: No recibí nada, quizás John sí.

sideB.text: I didn't receive anything, maybe John did.
I didn't get anything, maybe John did.
Nothing came to me, maybe John got it.

cards.sideA: Él lo recibió, yo no.

sideB.text: He received it, I didn't.
He got it, I didn't.
He received it, but I didn't.

cards.sideA: Ella lo ha recibido, yo no.

sideB.text: She has received it, I haven't.
She has gotten it, I haven't.
She has received it, but I haven't.

cards.sideA: No me dijeron que el precio iba a cambiar.

sideB.text: I wasn't told the price would change.
Nobody told me the price was going to change.
They didn't tell me the price would change.
I wasn't told that the price was about to change.

cards.note: [Was about to change] presents the change as imminent, on the point of happening. [Would change] and [was going to change] only place it somewhere in the future without that urgency.

cards.sideA: No me avisaron de la reunión.

sideB.text: I wasn't told about the meeting.
Nobody told me about the meeting.
I wasn't informed about the meeting.
They didn't tell me about the meeting.

cards.sideA: No me dijeron que cambiara la forma de hacer las cosas.

sideB.text: I wasn't told to change the way I do things.
Nobody told me to change the way I do things.
I wasn't asked to change the way I do things.
They didn't tell me to change the way I do things.

cards.sideA: Solo necesito un resumen rápido, para entrar en corriente.

sideB.text: I just need a quick recap to catch me up.
Just give me a quick rundown to bring me up to speed.
I just need the cliff notes to get up to date.
I just need a quick summary.

cards.sideA: La versión contra la cual se compila la app debe ser estable.

sideB.text: The version against which the app is compiled must be stable.
The version that the app is compiled against must be stable.
The version the app is compiled against must be stable.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~The version against the app is compiled must be stable~ is impossible because the preposition [against] is left without an object. When a preposition sits immediately before the relative pronoun, that pronoun is obligatory and can never be dropped: [against which].

The everyday spoken alternative is to send the preposition to the end of the clause, which is when [that] becomes possible or the pronoun can disappear: [the version that the app is compiled against] or [the version the app is compiled against].

cards.sideA: El servidor en el cual corre la base de datos falló.

sideB.text: The server on which the database runs crashed.
The server that the database runs on crashed.
The server the database runs on crashed.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~The server on the database runs crashed~ leaves [on] hanging with no object, and it also makes it sound as if the database were sitting on top of something. The fronted form requires the pronoun: [on which].

Note that ~on that~ is banned: [that] can never follow a preposition directly. If you want [that], strand the preposition at the end, as in [the server that the database runs on].

cards.sideA: El tema sobre el cual hablamos fue aburrido.

sideB.text: The topic about which we spoke was boring.
The topic that we spoke about was boring.
The topic we talked about was boring.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~The topic about we spoke was boring~ is wrong because [about] needs an object right after it, and [we] is the subject of the clause that follows, not that object. The pronoun has to be there: [about which we spoke].

The fronted version sounds formal or written. In conversation you would move the preposition to the end: [the topic we talked about].

~The topic about that we spoke was boring~ fails for a different reason: [that] can never follow a preposition. Once the preposition is fronted, the only pronouns allowed are [which] for things and [whom] for people. [That] is possible only when the preposition stays at the end: [the topic that we spoke about].

cards.sideA: La empresa para la cual trabaja mi hermano es enorme.

sideB.text: The company for which my brother works is huge.
The company that my brother works for is huge.
The company my brother works for is huge.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~The company for my brother works is huge~ reads as if the speaker worked for the brother, because [for] grabs the next noun as its object. Keeping the pronoun fixes it: [for which my brother works].

Only [which] for things and [whom] for people can appear right after a preposition. If the company were a person you would say [the person for whom he works], never ~for who~ or ~for that~.

cards.sideA: La casa en la cual crecí ya no existe.

sideB.text: The house in which I grew up is gone now.
The house that I grew up in is gone now.
The house I grew up in is gone now.
The house where I grew up is gone now.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~The house in I grew up is gone now~ fails because [in] is stranded before a subject pronoun. Fronted prepositions always drag [which] along with them: [in which I grew up].

Both versions are correct English, they just differ in register. [In which] is formal and written; [the house I grew up in] is what you actually say out loud.

When the antecedent is a place, [where] replaces the whole preposition + pronoun block: [the house where I grew up]. Because [where] already carries the meaning of [in which], it is never combined with a preposition.

cards.sideA: Las reglas bajo las cuales opera la app son estrictas.

sideB.text: The rules under which the app operates are strict.
The rules that the app operates under are strict.
The rules the app operates under are strict.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~The rules under the app operates are strict~ leaves [under] with nothing to govern. The object of the preposition must be present: [under which the app operates].

This pattern is very common in technical and legal writing, where you will see [under which], [by which], [through which] and [within which] introducing the conditions of a system.

cards.sideA: La herramienta con la cual lo arregló fue una llave inglesa.

sideB.text: The tool with which he fixed it was a wrench.
The tool that he fixed it with was a wrench.
The tool he fixed it with was a wrench.

cards.note:
**[er:232]**

~The tool with he fixed it was a wrench~ is broken because [with] is looking for its object and finds the subject [he] instead. You need [with which he fixed it].

In speech the natural choice is almost always the stranded version: [the tool he fixed it with]. Save the fronted form for documentation and formal reports.
